frames.narration: A shop app has orders, invoices and customers, built as three layers: controller, service, repository, one file per feature in each. That is 9 files, and a request for one feature passes through 3 of them.

Product asks to rename an invoice column. But the controller formats that column and the service builds a query with its name, so all 3 invoice files are edited, with 3 unrelated behaviours beside the change. The layers leak.

The team moves the column name behind the repository. The same rename now edits 1 file, InvoicesRepository, with 1 unrelated behaviour (the engine details) beside it. The boundary hides something, so the change stays below it.
An architect adds a facade, a manager and a domain model. Seven layers, 21 files. Adding one field to an order now edits 7 files, and 4 of them only copy the field on to the next layer.

Another camp prefers one vertical slice per feature: 3 files, each with screen, rule and query code. Adding a field or changing a discount rule edits 1 file, with 2 or 3 unrelated behaviours beside the change.

Then the team swaps the database engine. With slices every one of the 3 slices is edited, and 9 unrelated behaviours sit next to the change. With clean layers it is 3 repositories and 3 unrelated behaviours. The cut that helped feature work hurts here.

Over five typical changes the totals are: leaky layers 13 files edited, clean layers 10, slices 9, seven layers 17. Unrelated behaviour in edited files: 12, 5, 26 and 7. Tests re-run: 20, 20, 9 and 42. No design wins every column.
So choose the cut by the changes you really see. Keep a layer only if it hides a detail from the code above it, and be ready to move code between layers and slices when the changes change.
